title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Hits $100M Global Box Office, First Documentary to Reach 1M Letterboxd Views
body:
The A24 documentary *You Can See Everything*, co‑directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, has broken through a financial and cultural barrier that few nonfiction films ever reach: it has now earned more than $100 million worldwide and logged over one million views on the social‑media platform Letterboxd. The milestone marks the first time a documentary has crossed both thresholds, cementing the film’s status as a rare box‑office phenomenon while keeping the public’s fascination with former Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes alive well into its sixth week of domestic release.

The film’s ascent has been anything but conventional. Rather than relying on a traditional theatrical rollout, A24 paired limited‑release screenings in major markets with a strategic digital push that capitalized on the lingering intrigue surrounding the Theranos scandal. Early buzz on streaming services and word‑of‑mouth recommendations on film‑enthusiast sites helped the documentary maintain a steady flow of ticket sales, ultimately propelling it past the $100 million mark—a figure typically reserved for high‑budget narrative features. Its performance places *You Can See Everything* alongside a select group of nonfiction titles such as *Fahrenheit 9/11* and *March of the Penguins*, which previously achieved comparable commercial success.

Critical reception has mirrored the audience’s enthusiasm. Reviewers have praised the filmmakers’ ability to blend investigative journalism with a cinematic style that feels both intimate and expansive. By interweaving archival footage, courtroom excerpts, and personal interviews, the documentary paints a nuanced portrait of Holmes that goes beyond the headlines of fraud and deception. Fielder’s background in comedy and Oppenheim’s experience with true‑crime storytelling converge to produce a narrative that is as compelling as it is unsettling, prompting viewers to reconsider the broader implications of Silicon Valley’s “move fast and break things” mantra.

The film’s impact extends beyond box‑office numbers. Its record‑setting presence on Letterboxd—where it became the first documentary to surpass one million watches—signals a shift in how audiences discover and discuss nonfiction content. The platform, traditionally dominated by narrative cinema, now serves as a barometer for documentary popularity, suggesting that viewers are seeking deeper, more investigative storytelling in an era saturated with quick‑hit streaming fare. This digital footprint has also sparked renewed conversations about corporate accountability, the ethics of tech entrepreneurship, and the role of media in exposing systemic failures.

Industry analysts view the success of *You Can See Everything* as a bellwether for the future of documentary distribution. The film demonstrates that with the right blend of theatrical prestige, targeted marketing, and digital engagement, nonfiction works can compete head‑to‑head with mainstream blockbusters. Studios may be encouraged to invest more heavily in high‑production‑value documentaries, especially those that tackle timely, high‑profile subjects. Moreover, the achievement could inspire filmmakers to experiment with hybrid storytelling techniques that appeal to both cinephiles and casual viewers alike.

Looking ahead, the documentary’s momentum shows no signs of waning. With upcoming awards season considerations and continued international rollouts, *You Can See Everything* is poised to further solidify its place in cinematic history. Its unprecedented financial and cultural reach not only redefines what a documentary can achieve but also underscores a growing appetite for in‑depth examinations of contemporary scandals. As the film continues to draw audiences worldwide, it may well set a new benchmark for how truth‑telling cinema is financed, marketed, and celebrated.
